title: When should state live in React Query rather than Redux?
description: Learn to distinguish server state from client state, decide where to store data, and avoid over-engineering with the wrong state manager.

data.text: The single most common state-management mistake in modern React apps is putting **server-fetched data** into Redux (or any global client store) instead of a dedicated server-state library. React Query, SWR, and RTK Query exist to solve a problem Redux was never designed for: caching, deduplication, background refetching, and stale-while-revalidate semantics for async data.

data.title: The fundamental split
items: **Server state**: data that lives on the server and is fetched asynchronously—users, products, orders, notifications
**Client state**: data that originates in the UI and would not exist without it—form drafts, modal open/closed, selected tab, sidebar collapsed
**URL state**: data that belongs in the query string—filters, pagination, search terms
**Cache state**: derived data you compute once and reuse—memoized selectors, denormalized views

terms.definition: Data that persists on the server. It can become stale the moment it arrives. The client's job is to fetch, cache, and keep it reasonably fresh.
Data that is owned by the UI itself—form inputs, UI toggles, modal visibility. It is not fetched from an API.
A caching strategy that returns cached data immediately while silently fetching fresh data in the background.
Storing entities by ID in a flat structure so updates to one entity automatically update all references. Redux requires manual normalization; React Query handles it via query keys.

data.text: Use React Query (or SWR) for anything that involves `fetch`, `axios`, or GraphQL queries. It gives you caching, deduplication, background refetching on window focus, retry logic, and optimistic updates out of the box. You write a fetch function and a query key; the library handles the rest.

data.title: Fetching a user with React Query
data.content: React Query caches by query key. Calling `useQuery` with the same key returns cached data and triggers a background refetch.

data.text: Redux (with Redux Toolkit) still has a place, but it's narrower than most teams assume. Use Redux when you need **complex synchronous state transitions** that involve many unrelated components—like a drag-and-drop canvas, a collaborative editor with operational transforms, or a multi-step wizard where state is mutated by many different actions.

data.title: React Query vs Redux: where each belongs

cards.title: React Query / TanStack Query
cards.description: Purpose-built for server state: async data that lives on a backend.
pros: Caching, deduplication, and background refetching are free
Devtools show cache status and query timing
Less boilerplate than Redux for data-fetching scenarios
cons: Not designed for complex synchronous state machines
Team unfamiliarity with query-key conventions can cause cache misses

cards.title: Redux Toolkit
cards.description: General-purpose synchronous state container with time-travel debugging.
pros: Predictable, serialized state mutations via reducers
RTK Query provides server-state support too
cons: Developers often put fetched data here by habit
Cache invalidation is manual—no built-in stale-while-revalidate

cards.title: Zustand / Jotai
cards.description: Lightweight alternatives for simple global client state.
pros: Minimal boilerplate, no providers or slices
Great for form state, UI toggles, theme
cons: No built-in devtools as rich as Redux DevTools
Less opinionated structure can lead to inconsistency

data.title: The hybrid reality
data.text: In practice, most production apps use **both**: React Query for server data and a small slice of Redux (or Zustand) for global client UI state. The mistake is using Redux for both. RTK Query bridges this gap, but many teams still keep RTK Query data and Redux client state in separate slices.

data.title: Where should this piece of state live?
items: Does it come from an API? → React Query (or RTK Query)
Does it only exist in the UI and never gets persisted? → Component state (`useState`) or URL
Is it shared across many unrelated components and mutated by many actions? → Redux / Zustand
Does it represent navigation or filtering? → URL search params
Is it a derived value from other state? → Selectors / `useMemo`, not a separate store

items.question: Can I use React Query for client state too?
items.answer: Technically yes—you can store anything in the query cache—but it's an anti-pattern. React Query's invalidation and refetching logic assumes data can become stale from an external source. Client state doesn't become stale that way.

items.question: What if the team is already using Redux for everything?
items.answer: Introduce React Query gradually for new features. Over time you can migrate existing API calls out of Redux thunks. Don't force a big-bang rewrite—data-fetching is where React Query gives the biggest win with the smallest risk.

items.question: How do React Query and Redux Toolkit Query compare?
items.answer: RTK Query is part of Redux Toolkit and shares the Redux store. It provides similar caching to React Query but with Redux DevTools integration. React Query has a larger ecosystem, more tuning knobs, and is framework-agnostic. Choose based on team familiarity and existing Redux investment.

items.question: What about Zustand? When does it replace Redux?
items.answer: Zustand is excellent for small-to-medium global client state. If your Redux store has many slices mostly holding UI toggles and form state, Zustand is a cleaner fit. If you have complex state machines with many interdependent reducers, Redux's structure still helps.

data.title: Key takeaways
points: Server state = React Query. Client state = component state, URL, or a lightweight global store
Putting fetched data in Redux adds caching and invalidation work you don't need to write yourself
Use comparison cards to decide: if it's async and from an API, React Query wins
Redux is still valid for complex synchronous UI state that many components mutate
data.takeaway: Choose the store based on where the data comes from and how it changes, not on familiarity.
